analysis.one_liner: Opens federal lands and waters to oil and gas drilling and rolls back air, climate, and wildlife protections.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to seven House committees and ten subcommittees, never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would open the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic coast, and Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing, approve the Keystone XL pipeline by declaring its environmental reviews complete, and restart the Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository. It would strip greenhouse gases out of the Clean Air Act, replace industrial boiler air-pollution rules, let states take over energy permitting on federal land inside their borders, cut drilling-permit deadlines to 30 days, and sharply limit citizens' ability to sue over energy projects. It would also repeal a long list of energy tax credits — for wind, solar, biofuels, and some oil and gas — with the revenue directed toward lower income tax rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: new drilling areas in the Gulf, the Atlantic, and the Alaska coastal plain, faster permits, fewer court challenges, and weaker air rules for their operations. Refiners gain streamlined permitting and potential new refineries on closed military bases. Nuclear operators gain a Yucca Mountain waste repository and faster reactor licensing. Coal-burning utilities gain replacement of the industrial boiler air-toxics rules and state-run coal ash programs with permissive federal minimums. Renewable and biofuel companies would actually lose under this bill, which repeals their tax credits and the renewable fuel mandate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, refining, and nuclear companies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the moratorium on oil and gas leasing east of the Military Mission Line and near the Florida coast in the Gulf of Mexico, and directs the Interior Secretary to offer those areas for lease.
Requires the Interior Secretary to establish a competitive oil and gas leasing program for the Arctic Coastal Plain of Alaska (ANWR), repealing the section of ANILCA that barred leasing there.

Deems the Keystone XL pipeline's existing environmental reviews complete, removes the requirement for a presidential permit, and deems the federal right-of-way and water permits issued, with a 90-day deemed-approval deadline for the Army permit.
Directs the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to approve the Yucca Mountain repository license application within 180 days and removes the statutory cap on how much waste it can hold.
Requires the Interior Secretary to act on oil and gas drilling permits within 30 days, and grants automatic approval if the agency misses deadlines.

Lets states establish their own programs to permit energy development on federal land within the state, with the state permit deemed to satisfy NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act, and not subject to judicial review or the Administrative Procedure Act.

Requires Endangered Species Act listing decisions to consider economic data, and states that no environmental law authorizes regulation of climate change; excludes greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of air pollutant and repeals the renewable fuel program.

Repeals 15 energy tax credits — including wind and renewable electricity credits, biodiesel and alcohol fuel credits, and some oil and gas and coal credits — and directs Treasury to reduce income tax rates to reflect the added revenue.
Extends eagle 'take' permits under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act to at least 30 years, and deems a permit issued if the Secretary fails to act within a year.
Requires nonattainment air-quality designations to be based on monitoring data rather than modeling, and lets downwind ozone areas petition for extended attainment deadlines.

analysis.who_pays: Communities near new drilling, refining, and coal ash sites would bear the environmental and health risks, including coastal states whose waters would open to drilling and Nevadans living near Yucca Mountain. Citizens and conservation groups would lose standing and procedural tools to challenge energy projects: lawsuits would be confined to the D.C. courts, citizen suits could be dismissed at the agency's discretion, and developers would be shielded from paying prevailing parties' attorney fees. Taxpayers would absorb the cost of the Yucca Mountain program and, per the bill's findings, over $16 billion in potential utility lawsuit liabilities the federal government already faces for failing to accept spent nuclear fuel. Renewable energy and biofuel companies would lose their tax credits and the renewable fuel mandate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities, conservation interests, and renewable industries

drawbacks.text: Repealing the eastern Gulf moratorium and opening the ANWR coastal plain to leasing removes protections that shield Florida's tourism- and fishing-dependent coast and the Arctic refuge's wildlife and subsistence resources; the bill would limit environmental analysis of the first coastal plain lease sale to two alternatives with a 20-day comment window.

Concentrating judicial review of oil and gas decisions in a single D.C. court, narrowing standing, barring most suits beyond 45 days, and letting agencies dismiss citizen suits makes it harder for affected residents to hold operators accountable when something goes wrong.

Excluding greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act and barring agencies from using the social cost of carbon would remove the federal government's main tools for weighing climate damage in energy decisions, a cost that falls on the public rather than on emitters.

Repealing the plug-in vehicle, fuel cell vehicle, and renewable electricity credits all at once would sharply raise effective costs for renewable and electric-vehicle industries without a transition, even though the free-market design and revenue-based rate cuts have a defensible rationale.

Replacing the industrial boiler air-toxics rules with looser standards and allowing state coal ash permit programs to skip criteria the state deems unnecessary weakens limits on hazardous air pollutants and on coal waste stored near communities and water supplies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has some genuinely two-sided elements — it repeals tax preferences for fossil, renewable, and nuclear energy alike and promises lower tax rates with the revenue, and it addresses a real problem (the stalled Yucca Mountain repository that utilities have paid into for decades). But its dominant mechanism is transferring access to federal lands, waters, and permitting discretion to energy companies while closing off the courts, narrowing environmental review, and removing climate authority. For ordinary people the promised offset is cheaper fuel and some jobs; the certain costs are weakened environmental protection, reduced legal recourse, and concentrated public resources put at industry's disposal. On balance the design serves the industry far more directly than the consumer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2014, split across seven full committees and ten subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up; it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Duncan (R-SC) introduced the EXPAND Act on January 16, 2014, with an initial list of Republican cosponsors including Reps. Roe, Westmoreland, Wilson, Mulvaney, Gowdy, Weber, Poe, Kingston, Gohmert, Rokita, and Stutzman.

The same day, the House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee plus six others — Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Ways and Means, Agriculture, Armed Services, and Oversight and Government Reform — with the timing of consideration left to be determined by the Speaker.

Over the following five months it was further referred to ten subcommittees, including Energy and Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, Water Resources and Environment, and Readiness.

The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action; the last referral was on June 20, 2014, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the eastern Gulf drilling moratorium, ANWR's protection from leasing, the Clean Air Act's authority over greenhouse gases, the renewable fuel standard, and the energy tax credits all remained in place — so communities on the Florida and Atlantic coasts, conservation interests, and renewable and biofuel industries are better off than they would have been under the bill. Oil and gas, coal, and refining companies did not gain the expanded access and loosened rules it would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities and conservation rules stayed intact

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was from the Republican sponsor and 21 Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsor and no recorded Democratic action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's core would hand the industry new federal drilling areas in the eastern Gulf, the Atlantic, and ANWR's coastal plain, 30-day permit deadlines, and narrow court review — while the promised consumer benefit (cheaper fuel) is indirect and uncertain. The public would bear the environmental risk on publicly owned waters and lands.

The bill replaces the industrial boiler air-toxics standards with looser, cost-weighted rules, lets states run coal ash programs that may skip federal criteria they deem unneeded, bars EPA rules on coal waste at mines, and excludes carbon from air regulation — lower compliance costs for the industry, with pollution effects on nearby communities.

Streamlined one-agency refinery permitting and new refineries sited on closed military installations would lower refiners' costs and add capacity; communities hosting new refineries would absorb the local air and water impacts.

Reopening Yucca Mountain and speeding reactor licensing solves a genuine problem for a low-carbon industry and for utilities that paid into the waste fund; but Nevadans near the site have long opposed it, and the bill would remove the capacity cap based on the site's full analyzed capacity.

industries.industry: Renewable electricity, biofuel, and electric vehicle makers
industries.note: The bill repeals the renewable fuel standard and the wind, solar, biodiesel, plug-in vehicle, and fuel cell credits — a direct hit to these industries — though it simultaneously creates wind and solar leasing programs on public land and returns the revenue through lower tax rates, so consumers may gain some while the industries lose their subsidies.

The bill deems Keystone XL's environmental reviews complete, eliminates the presidential permit requirement, and deems federal permits issued, letting the project proceed on TransCanada's timeline; landowners and communities along the route would lose the remaining review and legal levers.
